# Time, Watermarks, and Progress {#sec-watermarks}

::: {.callout-note title="Status: complete first draft"}
:::

If a streaming engine has only one hard problem, it is this one.
*When can I close a window?*

A batch system can close a window because the data is finite: the
input file ends, the partition is complete, the day is over.
A streaming system cannot. Tuples can arrive out of order, sources
can fall behind, the network can hiccup, and a tuple from "ten
seconds ago" can show up after a tuple from "five seconds ago." The
engine has to commit to closing a window at *some* point — otherwise
it never produces a result — but committing too early loses data,
and committing too late builds an unbounded backlog.

Watermarks are the answer the streaming community has converged on
[@dataflow-paper]. A watermark is a promise: "no event with a
timestamp before *t* will arrive from this stream after this point."
When all upstream operators have promised a watermark beyond *t*,
the engine can safely close all windows that end at *t*.

NebulaStream implements this with a four-tuple of identifiers
attached to every `TupleBuffer`: `OriginId`, `SequenceNumber`,
`ChunkNumber`, and `Watermark`. Three of the four are *not*
timestamps. They exist because watermarks alone are not enough.

This is one of the longest chapters in the book. The mechanism is
intricate, and getting it wrong produces silently incorrect
results — the worst kind of bug.

---

## 7.1 Two clocks: event time and processing time {#sec-two-clocks}

Every tuple has, at least conceptually, two timestamps.

**Event time.** When the event happened in the real world. A vehicle
sensor records its speed at 10:00:00.123. The tuple representing
that reading carries 10:00:00.123 as its event-time timestamp.

**Processing time.** When the engine processed the tuple. The tuple
might arrive at the sensor's TCP source at 10:00:00.456, get parsed
and forwarded at 10:00:00.500, and reach a downstream operator at
10:00:00.600. Each is a different processing-time timestamp.

A query like `SELECT AVG(speed) GROUP BY vehicle WINDOW
TUMBLING(1 SECOND)` is ambiguous unless you say which clock the
window applies to. NebulaStream defaults to event time when a
field is named (`WINDOW TUMBLING(creationTS, SIZE 1 SEC)`) and
ingestion time (the source's processing-time stamp at ingest)
when no field is named.

Event-time windows are the interesting case. They are deterministic
across replays — re-running the same input produces the same window
contents — but they require watermarks to know when to fire.
Processing-time windows are easy to fire (the local clock decides)
but non-deterministic. Streaming engineers prefer event-time
windows almost always [@streaming-systems]; this is what we will
focus on.

---

## 7.2 The four progress identifiers {#sec-four-identifiers}

Every `TupleBuffer` in NebulaStream carries four identifiers that
together determine its position in the engine's progress lattice.
They are defined in `nes-common/include/Identifiers/Identifiers.hpp`:

```cpp
// nes-common/include/Identifiers/Identifiers.hpp
using OriginId = NESStrongType<uint64_t, struct OriginId_, 0, 1>;
using SequenceNumber = NESStrongType<uint64_t, struct SequenceNumber_, 0, 1>;
using ChunkNumber = NESStrongType<uint64_t, struct ChunkNumber_,
                                  SequenceNumber::INVALID,
                                  SequenceNumber::INITIAL>;
```

(`Watermark` is a `uint64_t` carrying the event-time stamp.)

Why four, not just one? Each addresses a different mode of failure:

**`OriginId`: which stream is this from?** A query joining two
streams has tuples from two origins; the engine needs to track
their watermarks separately, then take the minimum to advance the
join's notion of progress. A `WindowedAggregation` produces a *new*
origin for its output. Without distinct origin identifiers, the
engine cannot reason about per-source progress.

**`SequenceNumber`: which logical batch is this?** A source
produces an ordered sequence of logical events. The sequence number
is strictly monotonic, per origin. It is the engine's primary
ordering key; gaps in the sequence indicate missing data.

**`ChunkNumber`: which physical buffer within the batch?** A
single logical event from a source may not fit in one buffer. A
JSON record of 12 KiB exceeds the default 8 KiB buffer; it produces
two physical buffers, both with the same `SequenceNumber` but
different `ChunkNumber`s. The chunk number disambiguates them and
records whether more chunks are coming.

**`Watermark`: how far has time advanced?** The event-time stamp
beyond which no earlier-event-time tuple is expected. Chunked
correctly, this is the engine's key for closing windows.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 7.1: a single buffer's progress 4-tuple"}
A buffer freshly emitted by a TCP source might carry:

```
OriginId       = 7        # the seventh logical source
SequenceNumber = 152       # 152nd batch from this source
ChunkNumber    = 0        # first (and only) chunk of this batch
Watermark      = 1715000000000  # nanoseconds since epoch
isLastChunk    = true     # no more chunks for this sequence
```

A window operator reading this buffer learns: from origin 7, the
152nd batch has arrived in full, with no event-time stamp earlier
than 1715000000000 expected from this source.
:::

---

## 7.3 Watermark advancement {#sec-watermark-advance}

A source emits a watermark per buffer. The watermark is a promise
about all *future* buffers from that source: "I will not produce a
tuple with event time less than this watermark." Once promised, the
source is bound to honour it.

Sources use one of two strategies:

- **Punctuated watermarks.** The watermark is set to the maximum
  event time seen so far minus a slack `δ`. The slack accommodates
  out-of-order tuples within a single source.
- **Periodic watermarks.** The watermark is recomputed every *N*
  buffers or every fixed interval, with the promise being made for
  the period as a whole.

NebulaStream's source implementations use both, configured per
source type. The CSV file source, replaying historical data, uses
the maximum-seen-event-time strategy because there is no real-world
out-of-order; the file is what it is. A TCP source consuming a
live feed uses a periodic strategy with a configurable slack.

When a buffer with watermark `W` arrives at an operator, the
operator advances its local notion of "watermark for origin O" to
`max(current, W)`. For operators with multiple inputs (joins,
unions), the *output* watermark is the *minimum* across origins.
This minimum-advance is the engine's analogue of two-phase commit
for time: you cannot advance past origin O until O is willing to
advance with you.

The component that implements this is `MultiOriginWatermarkProcessor`,
defined in `nes-physical-operators/`:

```cpp
// nes-physical-operators/src/Watermark/MultiOriginWatermarkProcessor.cpp (sketch)
Timestamp MultiOriginWatermarkProcessor::updateWatermark(
    Timestamp ts, SequenceData sequenceData, OriginId origin) const
{
    for (size_t originIndex = 0; originIndex < origins.size(); ++originIndex) {
        if (origins[originIndex] == origin) {
            watermarkProcessors[originIndex]->emplace(sequenceData, ts.getRawValue());
        }
    }
    return getCurrentWatermark();  // returns min across all origins
}
```

Each origin has its own `NonBlockingMonotonicSeqQueue` —
NebulaStream's lock-free ordered-queue primitive — that
maintains the contiguous-prefix invariant we discussed in
@sec-seq-windows. A `getCurrentWatermark()` call walks the
queues, takes each origin's contiguous-prefix watermark, and
returns the minimum. This is the engine's distributed-friendly
progress lattice in 30 lines of code.

---

## 7.4 Why sequence numbers matter for windows {#sec-seq-windows}

Watermarks alone are not enough to close a window correctly. The
problem is that watermarks are a promise about the *future*, not
the past. A window that should fire at watermark 1000 cannot fire
just because some buffer arrived with watermark 1100; the engine
needs to know that *all the buffers with event times below 1000
have arrived*.

This is where sequence numbers carry their weight. Sources commit
not only to a watermark but to a contiguous sequence of buffers.
If the source has emitted buffers with sequence numbers 0, 1, 2, 4
(note: 3 is missing), the engine cannot close a window even if the
watermark on buffer 4 says "everything before 1000 is here." Buffer
3 has not yet arrived; until it does, the window is incomplete.

The engine therefore tracks, per origin, the highest *contiguous*
sequence number it has seen. Watermarks advance only as far as the
contiguous prefix allows. A non-contiguous gap stalls progress.
This is the engine's principal correctness mechanism: it prefers
to halt rather than fire a window with missing data.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 7.2: a missing sequence number"}
Source emits buffers with sequence numbers 100, 101, 102, then
104. Watermarks 100, 200, 300, 500. The engine's per-origin
state is:

```
contiguousPrefix = 102   # 103 is missing
maxSeenSequence  = 104
maxSeenWatermark = 500
effectiveWatermark = 300  # the watermark on contiguous prefix
```

A window that ends at event time 250 *can* fire (250 < 300).
A window that ends at event time 400 *cannot* — even though the
maxSeenWatermark is 500, sequence 103 might carry a tuple with
event time 350. The engine waits.

When sequence 103 arrives (with watermark, say, 400), the
contiguous prefix advances to 104, the effective watermark
advances to 500, and the window ending at 400 fires.
:::

---

## 7.5 Chunks and the SequenceShredder {#sec-chunks}

The chunk number handles a different problem: a single logical
event whose physical encoding spans multiple buffers. A 30 KiB
JSON record cannot fit in an 8 KiB buffer; it produces four
buffers with the same `SequenceNumber` and `ChunkNumber`s 0, 1, 2,
3, the last one marked `isLastChunk = true`.

The `SequenceShredder` (described at length in
`nes-input-formatters/README.md`) is the component that resolves
multi-chunk events. It accumulates chunks per sequence number and
emits the assembled logical record only when all chunks have
arrived and `isLastChunk` is set. It also drives a small piece of
state that downstream operators need:

```cpp
// from the watermarking design doc
bool seenAllChunks(OriginId origin, SequenceNumber seq,
                   ChunkNumber chunk, bool isLastChunk)
{
    auto& [lastChunk, numSeenChunks]
        = getLastChunkNumberAndNumSeenChunks(seq);
    if (isLastChunk) { lastChunk = chunk; }
    ++numSeenChunks;
    return numSeenChunks == lastChunk + 1;
}
```

This is the engine's per-sequence completion check. A window
operator that needs to know "have all chunks of sequence S
arrived?" calls `seenAllChunks`. The function is a few lines of
state per sequence number; in steady state, almost every sequence
has a single chunk and the bookkeeping is cheap.

---

## 7.6 Window types {#sec-window-types}

NebulaStream's window operators support three classical window
shapes:

**Tumbling.** Fixed-size, non-overlapping. `WINDOW TUMBLING(ts,
SIZE 1 SEC)` produces non-overlapping 1-second buckets. Each tuple
belongs to exactly one window.

**Sliding.** Fixed-size, overlapping. `WINDOW SLIDING(ts, SIZE 5
SEC, ADVANCE 1 SEC)` produces overlapping 5-second windows that
advance every 1 second. Each tuple belongs to up to five windows.

**Session.** Variable-size, gap-defined. A session window groups
tuples whose timestamps are within `gap` of one another. Used for
"all events from a single user's browsing session."

The window-type hierarchy is in
`nes-logical-operators/include/WindowTypes/Types/`. Each window
type knows how to compute, for a given event-time stamp, the set
of windows that contain that timestamp.

---

## 7.7 The build/probe split {#sec-build-probe}

A windowed aggregation lowers, physically, into a *build* phase
that accumulates state and a *probe* phase that emits results when
windows close. The build phase is keyed on the grouping key plus
the window identity; it maintains a hash map of partial results.
The probe phase is triggered by watermark advancement: when the
engine's notion of progress crosses a window's end timestamp, the
probe walks the hash map and emits one tuple per window.

The physical operators are in `nes-physical-operators/include/`:
`WindowBuildPhysicalOperator` and `WindowProbePhysicalOperator`.
A `WindowBasedOperatorHandler`
(`nes-physical-operators/include/WindowBasedOperatorHandler.hpp`)
coordinates the two: it owns the slice store, the watermark
processors (one for build, one for probe), and the trigger logic.

::: {.callout-tip title="Real-system reference: how Flink does this"}
Flink uses a similar build/probe split, with watermarks driving
window firing. The two important differences are:

1. Flink stores window state in RocksDB by default, not in memory.
   NebulaStream is in-memory only (Chapter 16). For workloads that
   exceed memory, NebulaStream relies on the operator developer to
   spill manually; Flink handles it transparently with state
   backends.

2. Flink uses a single watermark per parallel operator instance,
   tracking progress through that instance's view of the world.
   NebulaStream uses a per-origin watermark, allowing more
   precise reasoning about multi-source joins. The trade-off is
   bookkeeping complexity.
:::

---

## 7.8 Watermarks across workers {#sec-cross-worker-watermarks}

So far this chapter has described watermark propagation as if
the whole query ran in one process. In a distributed deployment
(Chapter 19), the operator graph spans workers, and watermarks
have to cross the wire.

The four-tuple progress identifiers we have been discussing —
`OriginId`, `SequenceNumber`, `ChunkNumber`, `Watermark` — are
exactly what makes this work cleanly. The information that
matters at a network boundary is *what an upstream origin has
promised*, not *which thread is processing what*. Promises
travel as TupleBuffer metadata.

When a `NetworkSink` (Chapter 19) ships a buffer over to a
`NetworkSource` on another worker, the buffer's metadata —
including the four progress identifiers — travels with it. The
receiving side does not invent new origin or sequence numbers;
it forwards the originating ones. A downstream operator on the
receiving worker sees the same `OriginId` it would have seen if
the whole query were single-node. The engine's notion of
progress is consistent across the boundary.

The implication: **a join on worker B between an origin from
worker A and a local origin behaves correctly** because the
`MultiOriginWatermarkProcessor` on worker B sees both origins'
watermarks — the local one directly, the remote one via the
NetworkSource — and takes the minimum. The minimum-of-origins
discipline that holds within one worker holds across many.

What does *not* travel automatically is *trust*. If worker A is
unreachable (network partition), the receiving side cannot
distinguish "A is slow and will catch up" from "A has crashed
and will never catch up." The engine's current behaviour is
conservative: a watermark that has not advanced is held to be
not-yet-advanced, and downstream windows wait. Chapter 22
discusses adaptive timeout policies as future work.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 7.4: a windowed aggregation across workers"}
A query reading from two sensors (sensor-A on worker A,
sensor-B on worker B) and aggregating into one-second windows
on worker C:

```
worker A: source(sensor-A) → NetworkSink(channel-1)
                                            │
worker B: source(sensor-B) → NetworkSink(channel-2)
                                            │
                                            ▼
worker C: NetworkSource×2 → AggregationBuild → AggregationProbe → sink
```

Two `OriginId`s flow into worker C's aggregation. The
`MultiOriginWatermarkProcessor` on the build side sees both;
the aggregation does not fire windows until *both* origins'
watermarks have crossed the window's end. If worker A's
network briefly hiccups, worker C waits — windows from before
the hiccup eventually fire when the buffers catch up; windows
that depend on data that never arrives stall conservatively.
:::

## 7.9 Garbage collection: when state can be released {#sec-gc-state}

A window's state — the partial aggregation hash map keyed on
`(window-id, group-key)` — has to be released eventually, or the
engine grows without bound.

NebulaStream uses a *slice* abstraction: state is partitioned into
slices keyed on a contiguous time range, and a slice can be
released once the engine's watermark has advanced past the slice's
end. The garbage collector (`garbageCollectSlicesAndWindows` on the
`WindowBasedOperatorHandler`) walks slices on every probe pass and
deallocates those that are guaranteed to never receive late tuples.

The decision is conservative: a slice is released only when *all*
upstream watermarks have passed it. Out-of-order tuples that arrive
after release are dropped silently. NebulaStream does not, today,
support late-data side outputs the way Flink does.

---

## Summary {#sec-ch7-summary}

NebulaStream tracks progress with a four-tuple per `TupleBuffer`:
`OriginId` distinguishes streams, `SequenceNumber` orders batches
per origin, `ChunkNumber` distinguishes physical buffers belonging
to the same logical batch, and `Watermark` carries the event-time
promise. Watermarks advance through the operator graph by
minimum-of-input, gated by the contiguous sequence-number prefix to
ensure no missing batch is masked by a later watermark. Multi-chunk
events are reassembled by the `SequenceShredder`. Window operators
split into build and probe phases, with watermarks triggering
probe and slice-based garbage collection releasing closed-window
state. The mechanism is intricate but conservative: when in doubt,
the engine waits.

---

## Reading exercises {#sec-ch7-exercises}

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 7.1: trace a window firing"}
Run a windowed-aggregation systest in TRACE mode:

```shell
cmake-build-debug/systest/systest \
    -t nes-systests/windows/SlidingWindowsWithGap.test:1 \
    -- --logging.level=TRACE
```

Identify the log lines that show watermark advancement,
sequence-number gaps (if any), and window fires. How many
windows fire over the test's lifetime?
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 7.2: introduce out-of-order data"}
Modify a tumbling-window test's input to introduce
out-of-order events (event times 1, 2, 3, 5, 4, 6, …). What
happens? Where does the engine handle the out-of-order? Look at
the source's watermark generation strategy.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 7.3: drop a sequence"}
In a copy of an input file, remove the third record from a
sliding-window test. Now sequence numbers are 1, 2, 4, 5, ….
Watch what happens: the engine should stall (no windows fire)
because the contiguous prefix never advances past 2. How does
the engine recover? Hint: it does not, automatically. The user
or framework has to provide a heartbeat or end-of-stream signal.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 7.4: build a multi-source watermark"}
Run a join systest:

```shell
cmake-build-debug/systest/systest \
    -t nes-systests/operator/join/JoinMultipleStreams.test:1 \
    -- --logging.level=TRACE
```

The join has two input origins. Trace the watermarks: when does
the join's output watermark advance? You should see the
minimum-across-origins behaviour clearly.
:::
